from: Allow Céline to explain the “inner child:”
first: That song always brings some tears to my eyes as it connects me with that original innocence the world wants us to beat down. Once I started feeling the world’s oppression, at age 12, I would listen to Suzanne Vega’s The Queen and the Soldier every night because, it reliably got the tears out (while it summed up the human situat

from: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
first: Céline’s song is called On ne change pas--“we don’t change.” I think that’s both fortunately, and unfortunately, true for most of us. Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding.

from: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
first: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Check if you can pause before you act.

from: Your Body Might Need Some Love First
first: If you notice tension in your solar plexus or abdomen, or anywhere else that seems to be keeping you from relaxing into that heart chakra love, try some non-forced, slower exhales and a little gentle self-massage. I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a yin-yang symbol, as well as gentle circular or varied directi

from: When Therapy Stirs Things Up
first: Some somatic work or reparenting therapy can feel pleasant, and some can feel like a raging storm got unleashed. It can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes nightmares later on as the memories begin to unwind.

from: Notice the Part That Came Here
first: Some people hear all this about loving themself and answer, “No. I hate myself.” Like my friend Malia, who told me, “My inner child is just capricious!

from: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
first: I’ve been writing this whole guide as if everybody who tries it wants to take care of the inner child. Some people get a little rush out of making somebody scared or small, though.

from: Ill Will and Loving-Kindness
first: In one of the Buddha’s own accounts of how he woke up from identity, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it’s hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it’s not obvious.

from: The Spiritual Side of the Question
first: I try not to proselytize about spirituality, because I’ve made that mistake before, and I now see that it’s better to let folks find it when they are ready. But when someone tells me they want to kill themself, I consider the topic to be brutally opened by default, regardless of whether they meant to do that, because if they act

from: This human life is the most precious opportunity
first: In Buddhism, death isn’t an off switch, and it isn’t a new-age get-out-of-jail-free card back to the Divine Source. Repeated thought and intention shape the mind, and that keeps going through death and rebirth.

from: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult
first: Now, don’t tell anyone about this! I’m going to reveal my Magician’s Secret.

from: Don’t Sell Your Inner Adult To Buy An Outer Adult
first: If you still feel like a kid inside, somebody who seems grown-up can feel like salvation, and letting them do some of the grown-up jobs for you can actually help for a while. But they can know things you don’t and still be wrong for you to follow too much.

from: Borrow One Competency at a Time
first: A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age ( along with spirituality ), but it’s not just a foolish waste of time.

from: Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
first: Plenty of people are still at the putting-up-with part of reparenting. Even with little or no warmth for your little one yet, the relationship can start with the Protector’s plain acts and the warmth can come after, which feels backwards, because you’d think you have to feel it first before you could do anything for them.

from: Protecting them from yourself
first: Even if you mean well, things don’t always come out the way you hoped. You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack.

from: Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
first: I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up. Maybe sometimes that script feels warm, but maybe too often it feels more like a critic, or a warden with rules.

from: Reframing attacks as unskillful attempts to help
first: One of my favorite teachers, Mr. Rogers, gave us an excellent example of how to extract the sweet nectar of truth from what less advanced souls might recoil at.

from: Earning their trust, day to day
first: A new roommate doesn’t win you over with a speech on move-in day (hopefully, right?). The rent just has to keep showing up each month.

from: Love Can Start Before It’s Trusted ❤️
first: Sometimes the love is there for your little one and still feels unsafe to them, or safe for a minute and then not. Some researchers found a phrase for that: “ compassion-threat .” People in their study with anxious or avoidant attachment, or a tendency to be self-critical, reacted to compassion imagery like a threat, especially

from: If the Love Isn’t Coming Yet
first: If you weren’t loved well as a child, then the suggestion to “love your inner child” can sound like nonsense. Love them how?

from: Borrow Someone Else’s Love
first: When a good friend sits with you while you fall apart it does help you feel better. You call them again the next time, and they get a little better at it every time while you don’t.

from: Borrow Your Love For Someone Else
first: Sometimes it’s not that you can’t love in general. Your dog can chew up your good shoes and be forgiven before you’ve found the other one.

from: Shame can make you feel unlovable
first: Shame comes when you’re holding a dark secret. It might be a secret for someone else who abused you, because it made you feel dirty or worthless.

from: How to Forgive Without Forgetting
first: One major stumbling block to healing our hearts and accessing love is resentment. The cure for resentment is forgiveness, but it can’t be put on a schedule.

from: Show Up When Nothing’s Wrong
first: If the only time the Nurturer shows up is when something’s wrong, your little one can start to feel like they’re your job. Sometimes show up just to say “I’m glad you’re here,” and then enjoy them for a minute, the way you’d enjoy a little kid who wants to show you a rock they found.

from: A Smaller Doorway: Goodwill
first: Sometimes “I love you” is more than you can honestly say, especially to somebody who’s treated you badly. Even the usual whittled-down loving-kindness prayer, “May you be happy,” can feel like rewarding them.

from: A Bigger Doorway: Divine Love
first: This is what the Inner Guide can bring you to, which will be discussed in the next section after the foundational guidance.

from: The Inner Guide: Becoming Your Own Shepherd
first: As the Guide, you choose what your little one learns and what it gets to experience, and you hold standards, the way a good parent would. By the way, this job doesn’t have to be called the Guide.

from: Are you ready for the Guide?
first: Most of us need enough Nurturer and Protector first. Otherwise the Guide just overrules your little one in the name of something higher ( spiritual bypassing , dressed up as direction).

from: Between Spoiling and Clamping Down
first: Maybe you’ve let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real. Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins?

from: Borrow the Guide to Build It
to: Borrow a Guide to Build It
first: If you don’t feel like the wisest apple on the tree just yet, that’s perfectly fine, because we can borrow the guiding function to start with, and you can get better at it day by day. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great Guide.

from: Remember When You Already Did It Well
first: My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating.

from: A Healthy Mind Is Not a Perfect Mind
first: The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide). It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life.

from: Guide Yourself To Divine Love
first: When you wish someone well, what do you have in mind? Probably something like, “I want them to have enough to eat, a safe place to sleep, some people who like them, etc.” Wanting this for someone is a form of love (this is the kind babies already understand).

from: You Belong Everywhere and Nowhere
first: The Guide points beyond itself, toward somewhere you belong that doesn’t ask you to give up being yourself. That might be nature, or existence itself (or nibbana , beyond belonging).

from: When the Spiritual Relationship Hurts
first: If a spiritual teacher you trusted betrayed you, even sitting down to meditate can feel like it belongs to them now. But if you let an abuser control your appreciation of life, then you’ve given them an unearned win.

from: Practicing With Your Little One
Start With Whatever Showed Up
first: Remember what we learned in “Noticing Counts” above. You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you’ve been staring at the rug.

from: You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
first: If you don’t hear a little kid talking in your head, don’t invent one. Actually, this is one place where the usual inner-child prompt to “ask your little one what they need” can get confusing, because “ask” sounds like you’re supposed to ask a question and then wait for a second voice to answer.

from: Use Childhood Photographs Gently
first: My friend Cody had trouble imagining his inner child, so he started looking at photos of himself when he was young. That did the trick!

from: If it tells you to do something
to: If it tells you to act
first: I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too.

from: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over
first: Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming “ shenpa ,” and she says “ hooked ” is a more descriptive translation for that Tibetan concept than the usual “attachment.” You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. 💃🏿 Or you might notice it e

from: What to Make of a Passing Feeling
first: If what someone did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others.

from: Gentle Meditation and Mantra
first: If the hook is stuck a bit deeper in your mouth and you’re flailing around like a fish out of water, gentle mantra meditation or self-hypnosis (which overlap a lot) are some tools that can really calm your nervous system down. A lot of people find that a mantra they feel some heart connection to, repeated in their head or out lo

from: One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night
first: In the morning, begin the day intentionally, not just because the sun chose to come up once more, since we can’t count on that. 🫣 Here’s one way you might pl/orkfully start off: “Today I will neither be Peter Pan nor Captain Hook.

from: Close the Session and Return to Life
first: Without an ending, the processing can just start looping. So when you’re done, look around and say where you are.

from: Discovering and Healing Old Patterns
Use hindsight to “re-do” traumatic memories in a healthier way
first: Once you’ve got your cast of perfected future characters (from Borrow Hindsight) in your mind, you can also go back to earlier traumatic memories and relive them in a better way. For example, I’ll take one instance from my own childhood.

from: How should discipline have been done right?
first: While often it is obvious how a perfect parent could have responded, in my example, I’m not exactly sure what a perfect father would have done here. But usually what my dad preferred as discipline was a forced “time-in” via a “punishment hug”, and I feel like that worked well for me.

from: Answering the Strict Disciplinarian
first: A good routine, like yoga in the morning and a proper bedtime, still feels like lock-down to your little one when it’s done in a disciplinarian style. One exercise you can do to handle this is to go back and rewrite your responses to that strict disciplinarian.

from: When the Practice Gets Difficult
When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
first: A lot of people get stuck right at square one. You call up the Nurturer and try to talk to your little one, and you get silence or a numb feeling, and all of a sudden your phone or the laundry feels urgent.

from: Sometimes There Isn’t a Clear Child Yet
first: Reparenting assumes there’s a clear little one in there to love, and for a lot of people there is. But if you grew up somewhere you only belonged as long as you played somebody else, like a really controlling family or a strict church, the real one may never have had room to form.

from: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
first: Some people have the opposite problem, where it feels like they’re connecting with their little boo, but then they find out somehow that it was still pretty superficial. Dreams can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in the second half of the night’s sleep, if you wake up in the middle to meditate, as I’ve dis

from: When the Urge to Escape Arrives
first: The avoidant guard shows up when you get close to some painful memory or insight. Suddenly you’d rather have a drink, check your phone, or do anything aside from directly feeling it (even a yawn can come with an “I’m so done with this” feeling).

from: Physical Pain Makes It Harder
first: Physical pain can bring on the urge to escape, and it can tie into emotional issues. Say an attack has you curled up on the bathroom floor, and whatever knocked the pain out last time (say, fent, or ketamine) starts looking real good, though you know it’ll leave you worse if you keep resorting to that quick fix.

from: Listen To Your Body, Or Else!
first: Sometimes, a physical illness is really partly or wholly an emotional issue, as happened to various friends of mine, including a med student friend who was going to the ER every couple days with undiagnosable phantom issues like paralysis and excruciating neck pain. One doctor finally told him it might be “somatic symptoms”, so

from: When Healing Turns Into Checking
first: Ironically, you can get hooked on healing too, which is actually still not healing at all. The wound can be completely real while you’re checking it for the hundredth time to see whether you’ve finally grieved it correctly.

from: How Would You Know It’s Helping?
first: Don’t be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself, “What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it’s helping?” This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, bu

from: When to Change the Strategy
first: Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I’d want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never have to find out what’s underneath this.

from: How many tries would I give it?
first: It’s not like we can just put a number on it. Some things shift in a day.

from: If you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results
first: Consider if you have a unique case these steps don’t match yet. Maybe you’ll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I’d do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with.

from: Altered States and Intensive Practice
Altered States Can Deepen Therapy or Escapism
first: When the physical or mental pain is intense and impenetrable, the urge usually sits on the fence between escapism and doing hardcore battle with the demons. Why not just blast right past that guard part, with intensive meditation or psychedelics?

from: For some people, reparenting starts feeling real in an altered state
first: Second gear, in this case, may refer to gentle meditation or self-hypnosis. When you’re ready, my self-hypnosis guide and lucid-dreaming guide can take those deeper, into third gear and beyond.

from: Everyone has altered states: Prepare now
first: In the previous section, I made it sound like you actually can put off intense altered states until you’re ready, but some of them are involuntary. Have you ever been attacked by a literal demon?

from: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
first: Sleep paralysis is a trance-like state, and trance can be “more scary” because you’re trapped in it, but it’s also less actually dangerous. In trance you can basically work with the fear.

from: When Escape Leaves Reality Behind
first: All kinds of psychoactive drugs can mess with your sense of what’s real, and that’s often the point of them, so you can break free of all your old patterns completely for a bit. But in general, try to select the healthiest ones and use slow and gentle protocols.

from: Is your paranoia a warning sign?
first: Paranoia during a rough trip can be a warning sign for psychosis, but it doesn’t automatically lead there, since it can be valid. It tends to go that way when it isn’t balanced by practicality.

from: If you might be prone to mania or psychosis
first: Any of those reactions, from mania to paranoia, can also point to a vulnerability in you, so I’d be careful with other drugs that mess with what’s real too. And any predisposition toward mania or psychosis is a warning sign too, whether it’s family history, a bad environment or a bad mindset.

from: Before you quit a medication or alcohol
first: Don’t suddenly stop a medication just because you suspect it’s involved. Talk to the doctor who prescribed it.

from: My Psychedelic Experiences Came A Bit Too Soon
first: The first time I took San Pedro cactus, at a medium-low dose, it made me super emotional, and I cried a lot. It was very therapeutic, actually.

from: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life
first: Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt by people that weren’t either of those, so some of the healing has to happen with real life other people too.

from: Rediscover Play and Your Own Preferences
From Survival to Experimental Play
first: If your childhood meant avoiding pain and keeping the people you needed close, your attention got used up reading danger (was that sigh about me?) and meeting their expectations, and when curiosity or mistakes got you punished, or it felt like they loved you less, you got better at playing the “chameleon”. 🦎 So early on, the pra

from: Let the Child Be Bad at Things
to: Let the Child Be Bad at It
first: Reflection can show you what got sMothered/suppressed. For identity development, you also need some experiments out in real life, so go try something new just for you.

from: Differentiation: Keeping Your Own Ground
Untangling the Belonging Bargains
first: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from what I call the “belonging bargains” which pull you away from your own inner-knowing in return for belonging. Your friends probably have unwritten rules about what you can joke about or get upset about.

from: Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child
first: Pema Chödrön has a quick map for finding the bargain. It’s four pairs, starting with pleasure and pain, and gain and loss.

from: Taking a Break From a Family, Group, or Relationship
first: Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. Sometimes you need to take a break from a family, group or relationship, even if they aren’t doing anything to you.

from: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone
first: Some families run on a bargain like “If I’m happy while someone I love is suffering, I’m abandoning them.” That’s exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfis

from: Finding People and Building Trust
first: I can’t tell you where to look for people who fit you, but I’d bet on more than one place. Keep the good people you’ve already got.

from: First Social Connections, Done Right
first: Once you do find the people, getting to know them can turn into a kind of test--“First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Some people try to make themselves as lovable as possible, hiding their real feelings to do so.

from: Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
first: Then there’s the stuff that’s hardest to tell anyone, and of course that’s exactly what you need help with. Maybe it’s an urge that scares you, or something you did that could get you in legal trouble.

from: Ask What Kind of Company They Want
first: Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: “Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, brainstorm, or...?” Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time, if it’s obvious what they want. But as they say, “assume” makes an “ass” out of “u”

from: Hearthwork: Taking Turns Lending & Borrowing Adulthood
first: Hearthwork is what I call my peer-counseling framework, which combines various other frameworks I’m familiar with. The basic premise is, peers take turns of equal length to privately listen to each other with respect and warm, positive regard.

from: Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
first: Especially at the start, some people might need some professional help in addition to self-help and peer-counseling. First and easiest is to start with finding a somatic therapist, if that resonates, as per my Somatic Therapies Guide .

from: Inner Child Reparenting therapists
first: Inner Child Reparenting therapists do exist, and you can find them, although they often are not licensed, and I don’t know of any central directory, nor of any protocol they’d have in common (aside from Lucia C’s, in the Appendix). There are none which work with my guide yet.

from: If you want a licensed therapist
first: The best licensed, listed therapists you’ll find that come close will be doing Internal Family Systems (IFS), or Schema Therapy. I’ll talk more about those in the appendix.

from: Before choosing a therapist
first: Get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I’d especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences.

from: Speaking Up and Handling Conflict
first: It’s often in handling conflict that we see the real inner child jump out. So if you’ve been wondering where they are in a session, here you go, let’s pl/ork!

from: If Someone Has Actually Hurt or Threatened You
first: Even once, whether or not it brings up old stuff, get safe first, which is not a small thing at all, I know.

from: Speak Toward What You Are Building
first: It’s not so hard to understand that words have power. They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that’s something you’d like to be able to do or a relationship.

from: If You Really Did Hurt Them
first: Repairing relationship damage is easier said than done, and must start from genuinely correct motivations. Are you really sorry for what you did, or are you just trying to feel sorry because they’re upset?

from: Other Folks Also Have Hooks
first: Once you’re in your happy place, look at the other person too, and don’t go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one “no” or boundary of theirs that made you mad--after all, they’re allowed to say no to you. Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hu

from: If a Relationship Keeps Making You Feel Less Safe
first: Look at what each of you actually said and did, and take steps to ensure your safety. Then turn inward.

from: When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
first: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one (figurative) life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, or your youngest real child moving out.

from: You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
first: And the love you’re worthy of is the same love as back in “Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!”, the Divine Love that can start as a little spark of relief when you give thanks. That kind, whether you’d say it comes from God or the universe itself or your subconscious, was there before you could earn anything.

from: How This Relates to Similar Therapies
first: My reparenting guide is part of the larger reparenting and inner child therapy category. As far as I can tell, it was first developed in 1976 by Dr.

from: Internal Family Systems (IFS)
first: Richard Schwartz, who developed IFS in the 1980s, called one of his books No Bad Parts . Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so this guide’s notion of “meet the guard first,” would fit right in over there, although I focus more on keeping the inner child safe first.

from: Development of my framework
first: My inner child reparenting framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice. Later revisions also compare notes with schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT,

from: Original Teachers and Practice Resources
first: Daja works with inner-child pl/ork intuitively, through the divine Nurturer and Protector archetypes. Her work is less neuroscience and CBT and more direct archetypal practice, and the three grown-up jobs draw a lot from it.
